set.summary_en: RLGN learns testing priorities on partially observed temporal epidemic graphs using separate local-diffusion and long-range-information GNNs plus reinforcement learning from downstream spread. Its substantive epidemic study includes simulation across network types and contact-statistics-generated synthetic graphs, alongside a separate nonmedical influence-maximization task. It is not a deployed contact-tracing intervention, and performance depends on network difficulty and epidemiological shift.

set.abstract: We consider the problem of controlling a partially-observed dynamic process on a graph by a limited number of interventions. This problem naturally arises in contexts such as scheduling virus tests to curb an epidemic; targeted marketing in order to promote a product; and manually inspecting posts to detect fake news spreading on social networks. We formulate this setup as a sequential decision problem over a temporal graph process. In face of an exponential state space, combinatorial action space and partial observability, we design a novel tractable scheme to control dynamical processes on temporal graphs. We successfully apply our approach to two popular problems that fall into our framework: prioritizing which nodes should be tested in order to curb the spread of an epidemic, and influence maximization on a graph.

profile_caveats: Clinical boundary: all epidemic-control outcomes are simulations. Supplement D.1 explicitly says the authors had no access to live contact-tracing graphs; April 2020 anonymized high-level distributions were used to generate synthetic networks and activity patterns. No prospective testing/quarantine trial, diagnostic validation, observed reduction in human infection or patient benefit is established. Graph nodes and simulation repetitions are not clinical participant counts.

The first printed author is Eli A. Meirom; official HTML and the PDF correspondence line use Eli Meirom without the middle initial. The displayed byline follows the printed author line. All four authors have marker 1, NVIDIA Research, Israel. No equal-contribution marker appears.

The complete original publisher HTML abstract matches the printed PDF after Unicode ligature, whitespace and explicitly source-aligned line-wrap handling only. Wording, numbers, punctuation and meaningful hyphens agree; no lexical or mathematical difference was found.

The testing model assumes that a tested latent or infectious node is identified and removed from the graph; quarantine lasts beyond the episode. This is not a validated test-sensitivity, adherence or real-world isolation model. The agent observes all past graph interactions and test results, an information assumption that is stronger than what a deployed system may possess.

The source itself limits success to intermediate regimes: Figure S4 includes a network where all tested methods fail to contain spread, and Section 5.1 expects little advantage in extremely sparse or dense networks. Figure S1 shows deterioration under test-time transmission shifts; its caption describes higher test-time transmission while the horizontal ratio is printed as mean p_train divided by mean p_test. That directional-label discrepancy is not silently repaired.

Source metric discrepancy: main Section 5.1 defines containment using cumulative infected fraction below α=0.4. Supplement D.2 instead states α=0.6 for all experiments except three-community graphs, where α=0.4. Therefore a reported contained-epidemic percentage is not a single uniform threshold across every result. Figure 6’s approximately 60% training-curve description is distinct from Table S5’s three-community 53±13% result; no identical-run claim is made.

Source configuration discrepancy: Supplement D.3 says Table S6 includes 4% initial infection, but its first column and Table S7 say 5%. Main Table 2 evaluates healthy-node fractions after 20 steps, whereas Supplement D.7 describes 25-step episodes. These are retained as printed descriptions without inventing an unreported reconciliation. Main text samples transmission probabilities in [0.5,1]; Table S7 separately gives U[0.2,0.6] for its edge-inclusion probability-distribution row, so those differently labeled quantities are not automatically treated as the same parameter.

Large network sizes are 5,242 to 103,425 nodes, not enrolled patient counts. The group labeled real-world datasets includes a compartment-generated Portland network as well as social, email, collaboration and WiFi-based networks. Simulating disease on those structures does not establish fidelity to contemporary population contacts. At least three trained seeds and at least 100 evaluation episodes per model are reported; the source describes its errors as standard deviation of the mean, not clinical confidence intervals.

A general superiority claim is not supported across both tasks: nonmedical Table 3 reports RLGN 31.3±0.6 on Enron versus degree centrality 31.6±0.6, and 9.1±0.5 on CA-HEPTh versus 9.2±0.3 for several baselines. The selected Figure 4 is a mechanism schematic, not performance evidence or proof of optimal intervention.

The conclusion states that relying on k-hop neighborhoods may degrade performance when long-range correlations matter, and leaves generalization across graph size/correlation and privacy-preserving deployment to future work. No privacy guarantee follows from using aggregate node-neighborhood information.

set.summary_en: Influence analysis measures how removing a transition or trajectory changes an off-policy evaluation estimate, with exact computations for kernel and linear least-squares fitted Q-evaluation and importance sampling. Figure 3 distinguishes four expert-facing diagnostics using simulated cancer dynamics. The real application examines MIMIC-III acute hypotension with an intensivist: 1,733 eligible ICU admissions are downsampled to 346 training trajectories (6,777 transitions) and 346 evaluation trajectories (6,863 transitions). These are different sampling units, not thousands of independent patients. Flagging measurement and timing artifacts does not establish treatment benefit, remove unmeasured confounding or replace uncertainty bounds. Figure 5 labels the left example 28% influence while the prose says 29%; PDF author Leo Anthony Celi appears as Leo Celi in HTML.

set.abstract: Off-policy evaluation in reinforcement learning offers the chance of using observational data to improve future outcomes in domains such as healthcare and education, but safe deployment in high stakes settings requires ways of assessing its validity. Traditional measures such as confidence intervals may be insufficient due to noise, limited data and confounding. In this paper we develop a method that could serve as a hybrid human-AI system, to enable human experts to analyze the validity of policy evaluation estimates. This is accomplished by highlighting observations in the data whose removal will have a large effect on the OPE estimate, and formulating a set of rules for choosing which ones to present to domain experts for validation. We develop methods to compute exactly the influence functions for fitted Q-evaluation with two different function classes: kernel-based and linear least squares, as well as importance sampling methods. Experiments on medical simulations and real-world intensive care unit data demonstrate that our method can be used to identify limitations in the evaluation process and make evaluation more robust.

profile_caveats: The selected figure is a cancer simulation, not a patient-outcome trial. The actual clinical study is acute hypotension in MIMIC-III, not a sepsis-treatment efficacy trial: the authors and an intensivist investigate influential observations and possible measurement or timestamp artifacts in retrospective policy evaluation. Appendix 4.1 begins with 1,733 eligible distinct ICU admissions, then uses 20% (346) for policy learning and another 20% (346) for evaluation. Section 7.2 reports 6,777 and 6,863 transitions in those two sets. Admission/stay, trajectory and transition counts are different units; the large transition counts are not counts of independent patients. The study uses the initial 48 hours for long stays.

The clinical setup uses 29 state variables, 16 discretized fluid/vasopressor actions and blood-pressure-based rewards. The evaluation policy is the most common action among 50 nearest neighbors, not a prospectively validated treatment policy. Six transitions exceed the stated influence threshold 0.05; clinician judgments and edits in two illustrated cases do not verify that all confounding or measurement artifacts are resolved.

Source numerical discrepancy: Figure 5 labels the left clinical example “Influence of Flagged Transition: 28%”, whereas the adjacent text says 29%. Both are retained as printed; no rounding explanation or corrected value is invented. The right figure label is 12%.

The four selected cancer-simulation cases have reported OPE errors less than 1%, 38%, 8% and 23%, respectively. Those are illustrative scenarios under model assumptions, not clinical error bounds or performance estimates across real patients. Influence depends on both the estimator and the dataset, as Figure 4 demonstrates.

set.summary_en: Forward-backward learning combines conditional characteristic functions in a doubly robust Markov-assumption test, then increases history length to diagnose a suitable state representation. Figure 2 reports power and type-I error across 500 fourth-order diabetes-calibrated simulations, not 500 patients. The only real application uses eight weeks from six OhioT1DM patients with type 1 diabetes, with 1,100 hourly decision points per trajectory used in analysis. Non-rejection first at order four does not prove the true system is fourth-order Markov. Offline value estimates enumerate 20 three-patient training/three-patient test splits and additionally average fitted Q values over simulated initial trajectories. The source reports no significant advantage over orders five and eight, and uses a one-sided 0.1 level for the other comparisons; clinical benefit is unproven.

set.abstract: The Markov assumption (MA) is fundamental to the empirical validity of reinforcement learning. In this paper, we propose a novel Forward-Backward Learning procedure to test MA in sequential decision making. The proposed test does not assume any parametric form on the joint distribution of the observed data and plays an important role for identifying the optimal policy in high-order Markov decision processes (MDPs) and partially observable MDPs. Theoretically, we establish the validity of our test. Empirically, we apply our test to both synthetic datasets and a real data example from mobile health studies to illustrate its usefulness.

set.abstract: Neural controlled differential equations (CDEs) are the continuous-time analogue of recurrent neural networks, as Neural ODEs are to residual networks, and offer a memory-efficient continuous-time way to model functions of potentially irregular time series. Existing methods for computing the forward pass of a Neural CDE involve embedding the incoming time series into path space, often via interpolation, and using evaluations of this path to drive the hidden state. Here, we use rough path theory to extend this formulation. Instead of directly embedding into path space, we instead represent the input signal over small time intervals through its \textit{log-signature}, which are statistics describing how the signal drives a CDE. This is the approach for solving \textit{rough differential equations} (RDEs), and correspondingly we describe our main contribution as the introduction of Neural RDEs. This extension has a purpose: by generalising the Neural CDE approach to a broader class of driving signals, we demonstrate particular advantages for tackling long time series. In this regime, we demonstrate efficacy on problems of length up to 17k observations and observe significant training speed-ups, improvements in model performance, and reduced memory requirements compared to existing approaches.

set.abstract: The true population-level importance of a variable in a prediction task provides useful knowledge about the underlying data-generating mechanism and can help in deciding which measurements to collect in subsequent experiments. Valid statistical inference on this importance is a key component in understanding the population of interest. We present a computationally efficient procedure for estimating and obtaining valid statistical inference on the \textbf{S}hapley \textbf{P}opulation \textbf{V}ariable \textbf{I}mportance \textbf{M}easure (SPVIM). Although the computational complexity of the true SPVIM scales exponentially with the number of variables, we propose an estimator based on randomly sampling only $\Theta(n)$ feature subsets given $n$ observations. We prove that our estimator converges at an asymptotically optimal rate. Moreover, by deriving the asymptotic distribution of our estimator, we construct valid confidence intervals and hypothesis tests. Our procedure has good finite-sample performance in simulations, and for an in-hospital mortality prediction task produces similar variable importance estimates when different machine learning algorithms are applied.
